turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Monday, the fourteenth of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go. [warmly] Claire, what's on the board?
Three things. A de-escalation that got cancelled before it started. A Fed that might raise rates into an oil shock. And, downstairs in the Rabbit Hole, a jar of cabbage.
[chuckles] From the Strait of Hormuz to a jar of cabbage. That's a range.
It's all one story, actually. The price of things — what a price does once it moves.
[curious] Okay, sell me that later. Start with the oil.

So. The Gulf states and Iran were meant to sit down in Oman today, to agree a shared way through the Strait of Hormuz and tell the world shipping was safe. First real step down since this turned into a shooting war.
And?
[deadpan] And it was postponed. No new date. Oman's foreign minister said it was delayed, quote, in the interests of consensus.
Which means what, in plain English?
It means Bahrain didn't show. Bahrain hosts the American fleet, and it wasn't going to be seen bargaining with Tehran. You can't sign a six-nation deal with five nations in the room.
[sighs] So close, and then not. What did the oil price do?

Held. Brent settled around a hundred and four dollars a barrel, up nearly nine per cent on the week. And while the talking failed, the fighting finished a job — the Houthis took Mocha and the island of Mayyun, so they now hold the Yemeni side of the second oil gate, the Bab el-Mandeb.
Both doors to the oil, contested at once.
Roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil now moves under some threat. That's the number the whole week hangs on.
[thoughtful] And everyone reads it differently. Give me the room.
Tehran, through Press TV, says the Oman understanding, quote, in no way means reopening the strait. The strait is a lever, released on their terms.
Doha?
Al Jazeera runs the diplomacy and the doubt together — one piece asking whether the Houthis can even hold that island. The headline was blunt: the escalation could flop.
And Beijing — the one with the most to lose?

[wry] Says the least. About half of China's crude comes through Hormuz, and its answer isn't diplomacy, it's diversion — more Russian barrels, more pipeline, less exposure to a sea lane it has no intention of policing.
Smart, and a little cold.

Here's the sceptic, though. The forecasters are fading the fear. The US Energy Information Administration still sees Brent nearer ninety dollars in the back half of this year, and the mid-seventies next year, as supply rebuilds.
So the bet against oil is really a bet that one of those two gates reopens.
Exactly right.
One more from the world desk before we talk money — Ukraine.

The short truce is over. President Zelensky said Russia launched around five hundred strike drones on the twelfth, hitting the west of the country. The pattern holds: a big meeting, a claimed framework, a strike within hours, the front line unmoved.
[thoughtful] Process standing in for progress. Alright — the money block.
Anything else on the world desk?

[thoughtful] Nepal. A year since the youth revolt that toppled the government, and now catastrophic floods on the Tibet border — a fragile interim administration tested by a disaster it can barely fund, with elections still months away.

This is where the oil comes home. Dear oil is an inflation scare, and the scare has flipped the market. Futures now put the odds of the Federal Reserve raising rates on Wednesday at around sixty per cent.
[gasps] A hike? Into a slowing economy? That's backwards.

That's the whole point. A rate rise into a supply shock the Fed can't actually fix with rates. The ten-year Treasury yield is up near four point nine seven per cent — highest since October twenty twenty-three.
And the safe havens?

That's the tell. This isn't a clean panic. The dollar's soft, but gold is bid, around four thousand three hundred and fifty dollars an ounce, and bitcoin is sagging, near eighty-one thousand five hundred.
So gold up, bitcoin down, in the same week. Break that down.

Read it through four instruments. Global equities — think VWRA — resilient but capped, near their high. Global bonds are the pain trade: yields at cycle highs are a headwind to the price. Gold is the regime's winner, bid on the stagflation-and-geopolitics mix. And bitcoin is trading as a risk asset, not a haven — soft into tightening.
[thoughtful] And the reminder we always give.
This is explanation, not advice. Forecasts are forecasts.
One local footnote before we move on?

The currency. Our own central bank manages the Singdollar rather than a rate, and its strong-dollar stance sits on the same tightening side of this oil story — a quiet defence of import prices. And notice the classic hedge is misbehaving: shares and bonds are falling to the same rate fear at once, which is exactly when gold earns its keep.
Now bring it to Singapore, because it's the same story with a coffee.

Two Singapore threads. One, the haze. The air went into the unhealthy band this month for the first time since twenty twenty-three, cleared on Friday's rain, and it'll be back — the dry spell runs into October.
And there's a law for that, isn't there?
[deadpan] There is. The Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, from twenty fourteen. In more than a decade it has never produced a single successful prosecution.
[scoffs] Never?

Never. Extraterritorial liability is worth very little without Indonesian cooperation, which hasn't come. The real tools are the advisories, the purifiers, and an N ninety-five mask. The law is diplomacy, not a cure.
What else at home?

The export print to watch lands Wednesday, and the ministerial pay debate closed — the Workers' Party backed the rise but kept pressing the one thing that bites: show us the real total-remuneration numbers.
Right. Tech desk. What broke?

China's answer to the chip ban arrived — and it arrived at Nvidia's price. DeepSeek has ordered about a hundred and sixty thousand of Huawei's domestic accelerators for a giant data centre in Inner Mongolia.
That sounds like a win for self-reliance.

Until you hit the wall behind the wall. The chip now costs around thirty-seven thousand US dollars — level with Nvidia's best — because the bottleneck isn't the logic anymore, it's the stacked memory around it. China can make dies for over a million chips a year and finish only a quarter of them.
[curious] So the sovereignty story is really a memory-yield story.
And the summit everyone keeps pointing at?

Xi and Trump, expected around the twenty-fourth. Expectations are low — the last meeting produced nothing on export controls, and the licences America did grant turned into zero actual deliveries, because Beijing quietly steered its firms to buy at home instead.

That's the sceptic in one line. And there's a home-lab footnote every builder should hear: the same memory scramble has quadrupled the price of desktop RAM in a year. If you're upgrading a rig, buy the memory now.
[laughs] Buy RAM now. Noted. Speaking of buying — the Kit.
Anker put a heart-rate sensor and a snore-masking microphone into earbuds you wear to bed. The soundcore Sleep Earbuds, the Pro version, three hundred and forty-nine US dollars, out in November.
Earbuds to sleep in. Does that work?

The idea's real — the wrist measures sleep from a distance, the ears sit where the breathing actually happens. But here's the sceptic: earbuds are a consumable, not an heirloom, and if you already wear a ring and a strap, a third sensor is redundancy, not insight.
[amused] So it's clever, and you don't need it.
That's the desk in a sentence.
And the Atelier — the buy-once pan. This one's yours, I know you love it.

[warmly] I do. Here's the whole thing in one idea: a pan is a sandwich of metals, and what matters is where the conductive layer sits. Fully-clad runs it edge to edge, up the walls; a disc base only puts it on the bottom.
And you can see the difference?
In the sauté. Clad walls cook the onions climbing the sides; a disc base leaves them pale. For copper, the grail is two and a half millimetres, with a stainless lining so you never have to re-tin it.
What's the money move?

Buy the maker, not the logo. Tramontina's tri-ply gives you eighty to ninety per cent of an All-Clad pan at under half the price. And the copper Paris has sold as Dehillerin since the nineteen-sixties? That's just Mauviel with a different stamp.
[chuckles] The white-label truth. Buy the three pieces you use, skip the boxed set.
Skip the set. Right — Theo, this next one's yours.
[excited] It is. Take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[laughs] Home fermentation. And Claire, here's the thing — three completely different crafts hide under one word.
Go on.

One, salt plus vegetables plus time — that's your sauerkraut, your kimchi, your hot sauce. Two, koji — which is the fun one. You deliberately grow a friendly mould on rice, and its enzymes pre-digest the food into pure umami. That's miso, soy sauce, sake.
So koji is controlled good mould.
[warmly] Controlled good mould that makes food delicious. The chef René Redzepi built a whole lab around it at Noma, the best restaurant in the world.
And the gateway for a normal person?
A jar of cabbage and salt. Ten dollars, bubbling in three days, and it beats anything at the supermarket. Then you fall in, and one day you're staring at a tray of fuzzy rice you made on purpose.
What does the gear cost?

Almost nothing to start — jars and salt. The one instrument worth buying is a pH meter, about eighty dollars, because the acidity is your safety line. The endgame is a German water-seal crock, the Gärtopf, that keeps the air out.
[skeptical] And the money pit?

[chuckles] Oh, it's real. There's a Hong Kong company selling internet-connected fermentation chambers that log the humidity to the minute. The community's own verdict is honest, though — a ten-dollar jar makes exactly the same kraut as a two-hundred-dollar crock.
So where does a nervous beginner actually start?

[warmly] Lurk first — read before you buy a thing. Then two jars, a scale, some salt, and a cabbage. Kraut in week one, a hot-sauce mash in month two, and only if you're truly hooked, the meter and the koji in month three. About twenty-five dollars to begin.
What about the fear? Isn't this the food-poisoning hobby?

[thoughtful] That's the great myth, and here's the sceptic. For a salt-and-veg ferment, botulism is basically a non-issue — the good bacteria drop the acidity past the danger line within days. The real risk lives elsewhere: koji grown too warm, and fish or meat ferments. Know where the risk actually is, and the fear goes away.
And the Singapore angle?
The heat cuts both ways. It's perfect for tempeh — that's a local heritage craft — but too warm for a slow kraut without a wine fridge.
[warmly] Okay, that one was genuinely fun. Culture and the body — quick picks.
Screen first. A twenty-four have a film called Primetime — Robert Pattinson playing a version of Chris Hansen, the To Catch a Predator man. Premiered at Venice, out on the twenty-fifth.
The sceptic?
Ignore the record-breaking-score headline — that's an opening-weekend hype number on a real, living person. Wait for the actual release.
On the wrist — the Good Life.
Seiko revived the design of the nineteen-thirteen Laurel, Japan's first wristwatch, with an enamel dial fired by hand, one at a time.
[wry] And the honest note?
You're paying for the dial and the history, not the movement — it's a workhorse underneath. And it's about a quarter cheaper in Japan, so it's a buy-it-on-the-trip watch.
The Family Desk — this one matters. A big new brain study.
The largest yet — over seven thousand six hundred children — found heavier social-media use linked to a thinner cortex. Scary headline.
[thoughtful] And the caveat, said in the same breath.

The authors say it plainly: it's a single snapshot, it cannot show which way the arrow points. Struggling kids may reach for phones, not the other way round. The psychologist Candice Odgers has been warning against the panic for years.
So what actually works?

[warmly] The boring thing. Change bedtime, not the birthday on the account. Get the phone out of the bedroom overnight. Sleep is where the screen really does its damage — for a twelve-year-old and for us.
Which is the Fitness desk, neatly. Exercise snacks.

One to two minutes of hard effort — a flight of stairs, some fast sit-to-stands — a few times a day. A twenty twenty-six review found it lifts your V O two max by about seven per cent. No gym, no kit.
And the sceptic, because there's always one.
[chuckles] The catch is doing it. Adherence falls apart in real life. It's a floor-raiser for the time-poor, not a replacement for real training.
Diary — what do we book?

The Grand Prix, the ninth to the eleventh of October, with the first-ever Sprint — the Killers, and Lana Del Rey's Singapore debut. Bruno Mars tickets go on general sale this morning. And Snow City closes for good on the thirtieth — do that one with the kids now.
And the Table?

The Maxwell chicken-rice legend, Tian Tian, opened its first proper restaurant at Jewel. A plate that's about six dollars at the stall is closer to eleven there — and that's the whole debate. Plus a Jeju-pork tonkatsu specialist in the city.
[amused] Twice as pleasant to eat, not twice as good.
[laughs] You always land on the price.
Which brings us to the Long Read — and it's a price story too. Australia.
[curious] Go.
Australia ran the world's toughest anti-smoking experiment — plain packaging, the highest tobacco tax on earth — and it worked. Smoking fell to record lows.
But?

But a tax is a price, and a price does two things. Below a line it deters; above it, it creates. Push it high enough, and the excise stops being a wall and becomes the profit margin of a black market.
[thoughtful] How big?

Illicit tobacco is now about forty per cent of everything Australians smoke. Among the youngest smokers, roughly four in five packs are illegal. There are around twenty thousand tobacco shops in Sydney — about sixty for every McDonald's.
[gasps] Sixty to one?
A legal pack runs up to fifty Australian dollars. Under the counter, as little as fifteen. When the gap is that wide, the arithmetic wins — and it's brought a firebombing turf war with it.
And can they stop it now?

[thoughtful] That's the ugly part. Cut the tax and you reward the habit you spent a decade pricing down; hold the line and you keep funding the arson. The same lever pulls both ways. The honest forecast is years of grinding enforcement, because a market that big doesn't unwind on a single budget line.
So the lesson.

It's the whole issue's lesson. A price is never just a number; it's a set of incentives with a life of its own. Set it high enough and people won't pay or quit — they'll find a third door. And it reaches us, because Singapore runs steep tobacco duties too.
[thoughtful] The word for it, by the way, is chop-chop.
[wry] Of course it is.
[warmly] That's the price of things, then. Oil, money, memory, a pan, a tax.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
[warmly] Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
